newsitem.title: CANADA: Court ends freeze on Friedland's Inco shares.
newsitem.headline: Court ends freeze on Friedland's Inco shares.

text.p: An Ontario court lifted an injunction on Tuesday on Robert Friedland's US$152 million worth of shares in Inco Ltd.

The injunction was requested by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, which claimed Friedland, an international mining financier, should be held responsible for pollution at a former gold mine in Summitville, Colorado.
"The evidence has led me to the conclusion that the liability of Robert Friedland is anything but clear," Justice Robert Sharpe of Ontario Court's general division said as he read his decision.
Friedland gained the Inco stock as part of Inco's takeover of Diamond Fields Resources Ltd, a company run by Friedland which discovered the huge Voisey's Bay nickel deposit in remote Labrador.

Friedland was also the founder and controlling shareholder of Galactic Resources Ltd, the company that controlled the Summitville mine and the firm which the EPA said is responsible for the pollution.
The EPA wanted Friedland's assets in Canada frozen since it said it has a strong case in Colorado to sue Friedland for US$152 million in costs to clean up the Summitville site.
The Ontario judge said the EPA's case was far from strong.
"In my view there are serious shortcomings in the case of the United States," he said, adding that the EPA had failed to show that Friedland was directly responsible for the pollution.
More importantly, the judge said, the United States did not voluntarily disclose all the relevant facts to the court, making it hard for the judges who granted the injunction to make a fair decision.
"A litigant that fails to make full and frank disclosure forfeits the right to an ...injunction," he said. "The extent of nondisclosure of the United States in this case is serious and fundamental."
A previous ruling from Sharpe ordered the United States to disclose all documents related to the case, not just the ones the United States had presented voluntarily.
Those documents showed the EPA had doubts about its ability to win the case against Friedland, the judge said.
Galactic mined gold at the Summitville mine in the 1980s using open-pit heap leaching methods where ore is placed on top of rubber pads and then sprayed with a cyanide mixture.
The area's rivers were polluted because cyanide leaked through the pads.
